title: Institutional vs ad-hoc arbitration - what clients should actually choose
p1:
Choosing arbitration to resolve a business dispute? Your next decision could save you months of frustration and significant money.

But here's something many clients overlook: choosing arbitration does not automatically mean choosing an efficient dispute resolution process.
p2:
There are two common options: institutional and ad-hoc arbitration.

Institutional arbitration operates under an established arbitration institution, which provides rules, administrative support and sometimes assistance with appointing arbitrators.

Ad-hoc arbitration works without an administering institution. The parties and arbitrator manage the process themselves.

Here's the surprising part: ad-hoc arbitration is not necessarily cheaper, and institutional arbitration is not necessarily slower. Poorly drafted procedures and disagreements over appointments can make either option expensive.
p3:
So, what should clients actually choose?

Institutional arbitration may suit complex, high-value or cross-border disputes where structured procedures and administrative support matter.

Ad-hoc arbitration may be suitable when parties trust each other, want procedural flexibility and can cooperate on appointments, fees and timelines.

One practical tip: don't just mention arbitration in your contract. Specify the rules, seat, number and method of appointing arbitrators, and the language of proceedings.

A carefully drafted arbitration clause can prevent disputes about how to resolve the actual dispute.
conclusion: If you were negotiating a business contract today, would you choose institutional arbitration for greater structure or ad-hoc arbitration for greater flexibility? What would influence your decision?
